claim: De novo variants (DNVs) are currently not routinely evaluated as part of diagnostic whole exome sequencing (WES) analysis in patients with suspected inborn errors of immunity (IEI).
source: De novo variants (DNVs) are currently not routinely evaluated as part of diagnostic whole exome sequencing (WES) analysis in patients with suspected inborn errors of immunity (IEI).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context for the study.

claim: This study explored the potential added value of systematic assessment of DNVs in a retrospective cohort of 123 patients with a suspected sporadic IEI that underwent patient-parent trio-based WES.
source: This study explored the potential added value of systematic assessment of DNVs in a retrospective cohort of 123 patients with a suspected sporadic IEI that underwent patient-parent trio-based WES.
evidence: This describes the study design and methodology.

claim: A (likely) molecular diagnosis for (part) of the immunological phenotype was achieved in 12 patients with the diagnostic in silico IEI WES gene panel.
source: A (likely) molecular diagnosis for (part) of the immunological phenotype was achieved in 12 patients with the diagnostic in silico IEI WES gene panel.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the diagnostic WES analysis reported in the results.

claim: Systematic evaluation of rare, non-synonymous DNVs in coding or splice site regions led to the identification of 14 candidate DNVs in genes with an annotated immune function.
source: Systematic evaluation of rare, non-synonymous DNVs in coding or splice site regions led to the identification of 14 candidate DNVs in genes with an annotated immune function.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: DNVs were found in IEI genes (NLRP3 and RELA) and in potentially novel candidate genes, including PSMB10, DDX1, KMT2C, and FBXW11.
source: DNVs were found in IEI genes (NLRP3 and RELA) and in potentially novel candidate genes, including PSMB10, DDX1, KMT2C, and FBXW11.
evidence: This is a primary finding listing specific genes with identified DNVs.

claim: The FBXW11 canonical splice site DNV was shown to lead to defective RNA splicing in primary immune cells extracted from the patient with autoinflammatory disease.
source: The FBXW11 canonical splice site DNV was shown to lead to defective RNA splicing, increased NF-κB p65 signalling, and elevated IL-1β production in primary immune cells extracted from the patient with autoinflammatory disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA splicing analysis.

claim: The FBXW11 canonical splice site DNV was shown to lead to increased NF-κB p65 signalling in primary immune cells extracted from the patient with autoinflammatory disease.
source: The FBXW11 canonical splice site DNV was shown to lead to defective RNA splicing, increased NF-κB p65 signalling, and elevated IL-1β production in primary immune cells extracted from the patient with autoinflammatory disease.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased p65 phosphorylation.

claim: The FBXW11 canonical splice site DNV was shown to lead to elevated IL-1β production in primary immune cells extracted from the patient with autoinflammatory disease.
source: The FBXW11 canonical splice site DNV was shown to lead to defective RNA splicing, increased NF-κB p65 signalling, and elevated IL-1β production in primary immune cells extracted from the patient with autoinflammatory disease.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements of IL-1β in stimulated PBMCs.

claim: The findings in this retrospective cohort study advocate the implementation of trio-based sequencing in routine diagnostics of patients with sporadic IEI.
source: Our findings in this retrospective cohort study advocate the implementation of trio-based sequencing in routine diagnostics of patients with sporadic IEI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The study provides functional evidence supporting a causal role for FBXW11 loss-of-function mutations in autoinflammatory disease.
source: Furthermore, we provide functional evidence supporting a causal role for FBXW11 loss-of-function mutations in autoinflammatory disease.
evidence: This is supported by the functional validation experiments showing altered NF-κB signaling and cytokine production.

claim: The biological rate at which de novo variants develop in humans translates to an average of 50-100 de novo single nucleotide variants (SNVs) per genome per generation.
source: The biological rate at which these variants develop in humans translates to an average of 50-100 de novo single nucleotide variants (SNVs) per genome per generation, only one or two of which affect coding regions (Acuna-Hidalgo et al., 2016; Lynch, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only one or two de novo single nucleotide variants per genome per generation affect coding regions.
source: The biological rate at which these variants develop in humans translates to an average of 50-100 de novo single nucleotide variants (SNVs) per genome per generation, only one or two of which affect coding regions (Acuna-Hidalgo et al., 2016; Lynch, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: De novo variants (DNVs) are often very rare or unique (absent from population databases).
source: De novo variants (DNVs) are often very rare or unique (absent from population databases) and have a higher a priori chance to be pathogenic than inherited variants (Meyts et al., 2016; Veltman and Brunner, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: De novo variants have a higher a priori chance to be pathogenic than inherited variants.
source: De novo variants (DNVs) are often very rare or unique (absent from population databases) and have a higher a priori chance to be pathogenic than inherited variants (Meyts et al., 2016; Veltman and Brunner, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNVs emerge between two generations and are subjected to minimal evolutionary selection pressure that would normally purify damaging mutations.
source: In contrast to inherited variants, DNVs emerge between two generations and are subjected to minimal evolutionary selection pressure that would normally purify damaging mutations (Acuna-Hidalgo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DNVs affecting nucleotides or genes that have been targeted by strong purifying selection can be highly damaging to their respective non-redundant biological functions.
source: DNVs affecting nucleotides or genes that have been targeted by strong purifying selection can therefore be highly damaging to their respective non-redundant biological functions, as has for example been shown for genes involved in innate immunity, an ancient host defence mechanism that developed under constant environmental selection pressure by microorganisms (Veltman and Brunner, 2012; Quintana-Murci and Clark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNVs are important candidates to pursue as a cause for disease, particularly in rare, sporadic phenotypes.
source: Therefore, DNVs are important candidates to pursue as a cause for disease, particularly in rare, sporadic phenotypes (Lynch, 2010; Veltman and Brunner, 2012; Vissers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of candidate DNVs can be assessed by trio-based sequencing, in which the patient is sequenced together with the (healthy) parents.
source: The presence of such candidate DNVs can be assessed by trio-based sequencing, in which the patient is sequenced together with the (healthy) parents (Acuna-Hidalgo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DNVs have been shown to constitute up to 50% of disease-causing mutations in developmental disorders.
source: Most experience with the systematic diagnostic assessment of DNVs has been gained in the field of developmental disorders, in which DNVs have been shown to constitute up to 50% of disease-causing mutations (Vissers et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2018; Kaplanis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The contribution of DNVs in the pathogenesis of inborn errors of immunity (IEI) is less clear than in developmental disorders.
source: However, the contribution of DNVs in the pathogenesis of other disorders such as inborn errors of immunity (IEI) is less clear.
evidence: This is stated as background context comparing IEI to developmental disorders.

claim: DNVs as the underlying cause in IEI patients have been widely reported in literature, but most of these mutations were determined to be de novo through subsequent segregation analysis and not by trio-based sequencing.
source: DNVs as the underlying cause in IEI patients have been widely reported in literature, but most of these mutations were determined to be de novo through subsequent segregation analysis and not by trio-based sequencing (Stray-Pedersen et al., 2017; Arts et al., 2019; Rudilla et al., 2019; Bradshaw et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IEI can present at different stages of life with a variable phenotype ranging from recurrent, life-threatening infections to immune dysregulation and cancer.
source: IEI can present at different stages of life with a variable phenotype ranging from recurrent, life-threatening infections to immune dysregulation and cancer (Arts et al., 2019; Bousfiha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In IEI patients with early-onset and severe complex phenotypes, there is an increased chance for an underlying causative DNV.
source: Particularly in IEI patients with early-onset and severe complex phenotypes, there is an increased chance for an underlying causative DNV (Veltman and Brunner, 2012; Vorsteveld et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNVs that arise post-zygotically or somatically are recognized as an important underlying cause for IEI patients with autoinflammatory disease.
source: Moreover, DNVs that arise post-zygotically or somatically are recognized as an important underlying cause for IEI patients with autoinflammatory disease (Labrousse et al., 2018; de Inocencio et al., 2015; Mensa-Vilaro et al., 2016; Kawasaki et al., 2017; Holzelova et al., 2004; Aluri et al., 2021; Beck et al., 2020; van der Made et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An international cohort study reported a diagnosis in 44% of cases after patient-parent trio sequencing, compared to 36% by single whole exome sequencing.
source: The potentially added value of systematic DNV assessment in IEI patients is supported by the findings of an international cohort study, which reported a diagnosis in 44% of cases after patient-parent trio sequencing, compared to 36% by single whole exome sequencing (WES) (Stray-Pedersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Trio-based sequencing has not yet been implemented as part of the routine diagnostic procedure of IEI patients.
source: However, trio-based sequencing has not yet been implemented as part of the routine diagnostic procedure of IEI patients.
evidence: This is stated as background context for the study.

claim: Patient-parent trios were selected for systematic DNV analysis when fulfilling the following inclusion criteria: (1) the patient's phenotype was sporadic, (2) the clinical description was suspect for an inborn error of immunity (IEI), and (3) the in silico IEI whole exome sequencing (WES) panel was requested and analysed.
source: Patient-parent trios were selected for systematic DNV analysis when fulfilling the following inclusion criteria: (1) the patient's phenotype was sporadic, (2) the clinical description was suspect for an inborn error of immunity (IEI), and (3) the in silico IEI whole exome sequencing (WES) panel was requested and analysed.
evidence: This describes the study inclusion criteria.

claim: The in silico IEI gene panel of the RUMC currently encompasses 456 genes.
source: The in silico IEI gene panel of the RUMC is periodically updated after literature review and currently encompasses 456 genes (version DG3.1.0 Radboudumc, 2021).
evidence: This describes the diagnostic panel used in the study.

claim: During the study period, the in silico IEI WES panel was analysed in 146 patient-parent trios, of which 123 trios met the inclusion criteria for the retrospective cohort study.
source: During the study period, the in silico IEI WES panel was analysed in 146 patient-parent trios, of which 123 trios met the inclusion criteria for our retrospective cohort study (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the cohort selection process and is shown in Figure 1.

claim: The selected IEI patients had a median age of 9 years (IQR 2–17).
source: The selected IEI patients had a median age of 9 years (IQR 2–17), and two-thirds of the cases were below 18 years of age (Table 1).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the cohort reported in Table 1.

claim: Two-thirds of the IEI cases were below 18 years of age.
source: The selected IEI patients had a median age of 9 years (IQR 2–17), and two-thirds of the cases were below 18 years of age (Table 1).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the cohort reported in Table 1.

claim: The sex distribution among IEI patients was roughly equal.
source: The sex distribution among patients was roughly equal.
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the cohort.

claim: Most IEI cases presented with autoinflammatory syndromes, followed by immune dysregulation and combined, predominantly syndromal immunodeficiencies.
source: Classification of IEI phenotypes according to the International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS) indicated that most cases presented with autoinflammatory syndromes, followed by immune dysregulation and combined, predominantly syndromal immunodeficiencies (Bousfiha et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the phenotypic distribution of the cohort.

claim: Eight IEI patients remained unclassified due to limited clinical data.
source: Eight patients remained unclassified due to limited clinical data.
evidence: This describes a limitation in phenotype classification for some patients.

claim: Potential disease-causing SNVs and/or copy number variants (CNVs) were reported in 36 index patients after diagnostic WES.
source: Potential disease-causing SNVs and/or copy number variants (CNVs) were reported in 36 index patients after diagnostic WES (Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the diagnostic WES analysis.

claim: Twenty-four patients were carriers of recessive disease alleles, previously characterised risk factors, variants of uncertain significance (VUS) or (likely) pathogenic variants affecting established disease genes other than those associated with IEI.
source: Twenty-four patients were carriers of recessive disease alleles, previously characterised risk factors, variants of uncertain significance (VUS) or (likely) pathogenic variants affecting established disease genes other than those associated with IEI (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the diagnostic WES analysis.

claim: Three patients carried de novo CNVs that met the diagnostic quality criteria.
source: Of note, three of these patients carried de novo CNVs that met the diagnostic quality criteria.
evidence: This is a finding from the diagnostic WES analysis.

claim: Patient 21 was diagnosed with an autoinflammatory disorder and carried a 17q terminal deletion of uncertain clinical significance.
source: Patient 21 was diagnosed with an autoinflammatory disorder and carried a 17q terminal deletion of uncertain clinical significance.
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the diagnostic analysis.

claim: A patient with non-syndromal combined immunodeficiency carried a de novo CNV involved in the Chromosome 22q11.2 microduplication syndrome (patient 69, OMIM #608363).
source: A patient with non-syndromal combined immunodeficiency carried a de novo CNV involved in the Chromosome 22q11.2 microduplication syndrome (patient 69, OMIM #608363).
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the diagnostic analysis.

claim: Patient 115 who was diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency carried a large duplication in Xq of uncertain clinical significance.
source: Another de novo CNV was identified in patient 115 who was diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency. This young female carried a large duplication in Xq of uncertain clinical significance.
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the diagnostic analysis.

claim: In 12 patients, (likely) pathogenic SNVs were identified in known IEI genes that (partially) explain the patient's immunological phenotype.
source: In 12 patients, (likely) pathogenic SNVs were identified in known IEI genes that (partially) explain the patient's immunological phenotype (Table 2, details shown in Table 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the diagnostic WES analysis.

claim: One patient with Muckle-Wells syndrome (patient 59) carried a de novo missense variant in NLRP3 (NM_001079821.2:c.1049C>T p.(Thr350Met)).
source: While most variants were inherited, one patient with Muckle-Wells syndrome (patient 59) carried a de novo missense variant in NLRP3 (NM_001079821.2:c.1049C>T p.(Thr350Met)).
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the diagnostic analysis.

claim: The NLRP3 variant NM_001079821.2:c.1049C>T p.(Thr350Met) has previously been described in patients with Muckle-Wells syndrome.
source: This variant has previously been described in patients with Muckle-Wells syndrome (Dodé et al., 2002; Jiménez-Treviño et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NLRP3 de novo variant (DNV) was classified as pathogenic.
source: Consequently, the NLRP3 de novo variant (DNV) was classified as pathogenic (Richards et al., 2015; Wallis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a classification based on ACMG guidelines.

claim: Routine diagnostic WES analysis provided a likely molecular diagnosis for (part) of the phenotype in 18 patients (14.6%) based on established mutational mechanisms and disease associations.
source: Overall, routine diagnostic WES analysis provided a likely molecular diagnosis for (part) of the phenotype in 18 patients (14.6%) based on established mutational mechanisms and disease associations (Table 2).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the diagnostic WES analysis.

claim: Automated DNV filtering retained a total of 172 candidate DNVs that were rare and located in either exonic or splice site regions.
source: Automated DNV filtering retained a total of 172 candidate DNVs that were rare (148 DNVs were absent from GnomAD genomes) and located in either exonic or splice site regions (the complete list can be found in Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: 148 DNVs were absent from GnomAD genomes.
source: Automated DNV filtering retained a total of 172 candidate DNVs that were rare (148 DNVs were absent from GnomAD genomes) and located in either exonic or splice site regions (the complete list can be found in Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: The total number of candidate DNVs among patients ranged between zero and six.
source: The total number of candidate DNVs among patients ranged between zero and six (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic DNV analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average number of candidate DNVs was comparable to recent literature.
source: Moreover, the average number of candidate DNVs was comparable to recent literature (Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies.

claim: Of the 172 candidate DNVs, 124 were non-synonymous and therefore expected to exert an effect on protein function.
source: Of these candidate DNVs, 124 were non-synonymous and therefore expected to exert an effect on protein function (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: Two pairs of patients carried candidate DNVs in the same gene, GIGYF1 (patients 49 and 83) and MAP3K10 (patients 98 and 118).
source: Two pairs of patients carried candidate DNVs in the same gene, GIGYF1 (patients 49 and 83) and MAP3K10 (patients 98 and 118).
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: Patients with DNVs in GIGYF1 and MAP3K10 did not share phenotypic features and the function of the proteins encoded by these genes could not be linked to the respective patient phenotype.
source: However, these patients did not share phenotypic features and the function of the proteins encoded by these genes could not be linked to the respective patient phenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Systematic evaluation of all non-synonymous candidate DNVs led to the selection of 14 candidate DNVs potentially causing IEI.
source: Subsequently, all non-synonymous candidate DNVs were systematically evaluated based on information on variant and gene level metrics, leading to the selection of 14 candidate DNVs potentially causing IEI (Tables 3 and 4), including the above-mentioned variant in the known IEI gene NLRP3.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: The 13 novel IEI candidate DNVs were found in patients with different IEI phenotypes, although three subtypes reoccurred: predominantly antibody deficiency (hypogammaglobulinemia), autoinflammatory disorder and bone marrow failure.
source: The 13 novel IEI candidate DNVs were found in patients with different IEI phenotypes, although three subtypes reoccurred: predominantly antibody deficiency (hypogammaglobulinemia), autoinflammatory disorder and bone marrow failure.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: A patient with an autoinflammatory phenotype characterised by mucocutaneous ulceration of mouth and genital area carried a DNV in RELA that was located in the canonical splice acceptor site preceding exon 10 (patient 119).
source: A patient with an autoinflammatory phenotype characterised by mucocutaneous ulceration of mouth and genital area carried a DNV in RELA that was located in the canonical splice acceptor site preceding exon 10 (patient 119, Table 4).
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: The guanine to adenine change in RELA was predicted to compromise the splice acceptor site by transferring it to the first guanine of exon 10, leading to an out-of-frame exon.
source: The guanine to adenine change was predicted to compromise the splice acceptor site by transferring it to the first guanine of exon 10, leading to an out-of-frame exon.
evidence: This is a prediction based on in silico analysis.

claim: The resulting frameshift in RELA was assumed to cause a reduction in functional RelA protein by nonsense-mediated decay.
source: The resulting frameshift was therefore assumed to cause a reduction in functional RelA protein by nonsense-mediated decay.
evidence: This is an inference based on the predicted effect of the variant.

claim: RelA is also known as p65 and is critically involved in nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) heterodimer formation and consequent activation of NF-κB-mediated proinflammatory signalling.
source: RelA is also known as p65 and is critically involved in nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) heterodimer formation and consequent activation of NF-κB-mediated proinflammatory signalling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of RelA/p65.

claim: RELA has been reported as an IEI gene in a previous IUIS classification but was not yet listed in the IEI in silico gene panel of the Department of Human Genetics because evidence was considered insufficient at the time.
source: Although RELA has already been reported as an IEI gene in a previous IUIS classification (Tangye et al., 2020), it was not yet listed in the IEI in silico gene panel of our Department of Human Genetics (Radboudumc, 2021), because evidence was considered insufficient at the time.
evidence: This explains why RELA was not included in the diagnostic panel.

claim: A private de novo missense variant in PSMB10 was found in a patient with Omenn syndrome with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), ectodermal dysplasia, alopecia, hypodontia and anonychia (patient 1).
source: In addition, a private de novo missense variant in PSMB10 was found in a patient with Omenn syndrome with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), ectodermal dysplasia, alopecia, hypodontia and anonychia (patient 1, Table 4).
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: The clinical phenotype of patient 1 with PSMB10 variant has been previously reported.
source: The clinical phenotype of this patient has been previously reported (D'hauw et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The PSMB10 DNV was predicted to be pathogenic based on the majority of variant and gene level metrics.
source: The DNV was predicted to be pathogenic based on the majority of variant and gene level metrics.
evidence: This is based on in silico prediction tools.

claim: The genomic location of PSMB10 was spanned by a partial somatic uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 (UPD16).
source: In additional data that was available from a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) micro-array, it was shown that the genomic location of PSMB10 was spanned by a partial somatic uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 (UPD16) (manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is based on SNP array data.

claim: PSMB10 encodes the β2i-subunit of the immuno- and thymoproteasome.
source: PSMB10 encodes the β2i-subunit of the immuno- and thymoproteasome and mutations leading to a loss of PSMB10 protein function have been associated with severe immunological defects (Treise et al., 2018; Sarrabay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSMB10 function supported by citations.

claim: Mutations leading to a loss of PSMB10 protein function have been associated with severe immunological defects.
source: PSMB10 encodes the β2i-subunit of the immuno- and thymoproteasome and mutations leading to a loss of PSMB10 protein function have been associated with severe immunological defects (Treise et al., 2018; Sarrabay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A candidate DNV was identified in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) due to a B cell maturation defect, auto-immune cytopenia, polyclonal T cell large granular lymphocytes in the bone marrow, recurrent viral infections, psoriasis and alopecia areata (patient 49).
source: Furthermore, another candidate DNV was identified in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) due to a B cell maturation defect, auto-immune cytopenia, polyclonal T cell large granular lymphocytes in the bone marrow, recurrent viral infections, psoriasis and alopecia areata, (patient 49, Table 4).
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: The frameshift variant in DDX1 was predicted to cause loss of protein function.
source: This frameshift variant in DDX1 was predicted to cause loss of protein function.
evidence: This is based on in silico prediction.

claim: DDX1 encodes a RNA helicase, which is part of a double-stranded RNA sensor that activates the NF-κB pathway and type I interferon responses.
source: DDX1 encodes a RNA helicase, which is part of a double-stranded RNA sensor that activates the NF-κB pathway and type I interferon responses (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DDX1 is involved in the regulation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell homeostasis.
source: Moreover, DDX1 is involved in the regulation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell homeostasis (Zhang et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A frameshift DNV in KMT2C was carried by a patient with a syndromal combined immunodeficiency characterised by recurrent ear infections, developmental delay, low-average intelligence level and facial dysmorphism (patient 78).
source: Another frameshift DNV in KMT2C was carried by a patient with a syndromal combined immunodeficiency characterised by recurrent ear infections, developmental delay, low-average intelligence level and facial dysmorphism (patient 78, Table 4).
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: The KMT2C variant was predicted to lead to a loss-of-function (LoF) of the KMT2C protein, which acts as a histone methyltransferase in the regulation of chromatin organisation.
source: The variant was predicted to lead to a loss-of-function (LoF) of the KMT2C protein, which acts as a histone methyltransferase in the regulation of chromatin organisation.
evidence: This is based on in silico prediction and knowledge of protein function.

claim: A DNV affecting FBXW11 was identified in a patient with an autoinflammatory disorder characterised by recurrent periodic fever and severe headaches (patient 53).
source: Lastly, a DNV affecting FBXW11 was identified in a patient with an autoinflammatory disorder characterised by recurrent periodic fever and severe headaches (patient 53, Table 4).
evidence: This is a specific case finding from the systematic DNV analysis.

claim: FBXW11 encodes a component of SCF (SKP1-CUL1-F-box) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, TrCP2, that is involved in the regulation of NF-κB signalling through the ubiquitination of several of its components.
source: FBXW11 encodes a component of SCF (SKP1-CUL1-F-box) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, TrCP2, that is involved in the regulation of NF-κB signalling through the ubiquitination of several of its components (Wang et al., 2018; Kanarek and Ben-Neriah, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An important function of both the TrCP1 and TrCP2 isoforms is the regulation of IκBα degradation, leading to subsequent activation of NF-κB and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: An important function of both the TrCP1 and TrCP2 isoforms is the regulation of IκBα degradation, leading to subsequent activation of NF-κB and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Kim et al., 2015; Yaron et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The identified FBXW11 DNV affected the canonical splice acceptor site preceding exon 12 (NM_012300.2:c.1468-2A>G).
source: The identified DNV affected the canonical splice acceptor site preceding exon 12 (NM_012300.2:c.1468-2A>G) and was predicted to lead to skipping of exon 12 based on splicing prediction by the Alamut Visual Software and to be deleterious by all utilised in silico prediction tools.
evidence: This is a specific variant finding.

claim: The FBXW11 DNV was predicted to lead to skipping of exon 12 based on splicing prediction by the Alamut Visual Software and to be deleterious by all utilised in silico prediction tools.
source: The identified DNV affected the canonical splice acceptor site preceding exon 12 (NM_012300.2:c.1468-2A>G) and was predicted to lead to skipping of exon 12 based on splicing prediction by the Alamut Visual Software and to be deleterious by all utilised in silico prediction tools.
evidence: This is based on in silico prediction tools.

claim: The predicted RNA splicing defect leading to an in-frame, shortened RNA transcript was confirmed in Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) transformed B cells from the patient.
source: The predicted RNA splicing defect leading to an in-frame, shortened RNA transcript was confirmed in Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) transformed B cells from the patient (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: De novo missense and nonsense variants in FBXW11 have been previously described in patients with a neurodevelopmental syndrome with abnormalities of the digits, jaw and eyes.
source: De novo missense and nonsense variants in FBXW11 have been previously described in patients with a neurodevelopmental syndrome with abnormalities of the digits, jaw and eyes (Holt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Previously described FBXW11 variants were located in WD1, WD4, and WD6 and have been shown to compromise substrate recognition or binding of the Wnt and Hedgehog signalling developmental pathways.
source: These variants were located in WD1, WD4, and WD6 and have been shown to compromise substrate recognition or binding of the Wnt and Hedgehog signalling developmental pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) extracted from the patient with FBXW11 variant, the phosphorylation of the NF-κB subunit p65 was constitutively higher in monocytes and CD8+ T cells as compared to a healthy control.
source: In peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) extracted from the patient, we demonstrated that the phosphorylation of the NF-κB subunit p65 was constitutively higher in monocytes and CD8+ T cells as compared to a healthy control, which suggests a functional effect of the FBXW11 variant.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Increased p65 phosphorylation and downstream production of IL-1β after stimulation with pathogens and a TLR3 ligand was observed in the patient with FBXW11 variant.
source: This effect is further substantiated by the observation of increased p65 phosphorylation and downstream production of IL-1β after stimulation with pathogens and a TLR3 ligand in the patient.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The results suggest that NF-κB signalling was aberrantly increased in the patient with FBXW11 variant, a mechanism that has been shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of other monogenic autoinflammatory disorders known as relopathies.
source: These results suggest that NF-κB signalling was aberrantly increased in the patient, a mechanism that has been shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of other monogenic autoinflammatory disorders known as relopathies (van der Made et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results supported by citation.

claim: The exact mutational mechanism that explains the different phenotype of the FBXW11 variant compared to previous cases with neurodevelopmental disease remains unclear.
source: However, the exact mutational mechanism that explains the different phenotype compared to the previous cases with neurodevelopmental disease remains unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in understanding the mechanism.

claim: The most likely explanation for the different phenotype would be a differential effect on the specific functions of the SCF complex that could be cell-type dependent rather than a difference in tissue-specific isoform expression.
source: The most likely explanation would be a differential effect on the specific functions of the SCF complex that could be cell-type dependent rather than a difference in tissue-specific isoform expression, since the DNV affects all three high quality protein-coding transcripts that produce the most abundant isoforms (Consortium, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotype.
